title.analysis: Authentic title "Why High-Yield Savings Accounts Are Making a Comeback in 2026" is a trend/timeliness frame ("Making a Comeback in 2026") with a curiosity hook in the form of a question-like claim. Against the frozen same-channel 10-peer cohort the video is 0.77044x (TYPICAL); against the 5-peer sensitivity cohort 0.75642x (TYPICAL); about 48 days old at snapshot. The script then rejects the title's premise ("It is not a comeback") and reframes it as a savers-finally-looked story, so the title is a hook the script argues against. Association only.

script.opening_words: Right now, somewhere in your banking app, there is a number quietly insulting you. My name is Nick, and if you bank with one of the three biggest banks in America, that number is 1/100 of 1%, which means my friend Yvette, who has loyally parked $31,000 at the
script.ending_words: ccount, and say it out loud. If that number embarrasses you, congratulations. You've just found the highest paying 15 minutes available to you this year. And unlike everything else in personal finance, this one doesn't require you to be right about the future.
script.analysis: Full 17518 canonical characters read. A persona-driven consumer-finance explainer: two named savers (Yvette at 0.01%, Curtis at 4.5%) frame a 450x interest gap; thesis that the "comeback" is not rates recovering but people finally looking; deposit-beta asymmetry; median-vs-mean household balance; per-hour value of switching ($330 on $8,000); inertia explanation; the Synapse cautionary tale (app-versus-chartered-bank); state-tax comparison of savings vs T-bills; an explicit counter-argument that cash is a poor long-term store; a five-point checklist and "say your rate out loud" close. Strong structure and mostly verifiable arithmetic, with candid caveats (rates move, Raisin is a seller, not financial advice). Weaknesses: the headline "first time in 15 years" contradicts the video's own 2023 rate (over 5%) and CPI; the $4,000 forgone-interest and 27% tax-advantage figures are not reproducible as stated; several statistics (FDIC average, SCF, Synapse, FOMC dots, Vanguard) are uncited and unverified here. Sponsor-like "school community" mentions.
beat_map: Hook: bank-app rate "quietly insulting you"; Yvette earns $3, Curtis $1,350 (450x).
Promise: "It is not a comeback. It is something considerably stranger"; rates-move warning.
The gap: best HYSA 4.5% vs FDIC national average 3/800 of 1%; 1/12 of what is available.
Inflation (3.5% June; core 2.6): Yvette's $31,000 shrinks ~$1,000 a year.
Rates fell, not rose: 5% in 2023, six Fed cuts, funds target 5.25 to 3.5; "tail end of a long, quiet decline".
Why people are talking: cuts stopped, inflation up, savings finally beat inflation.
Deposit beta explained; asymmetric pass-through; Deloitte "downwards flexible, upwards sticky".
Yvette's bank 0.01% through the 16-month hiking cycle; $10.2T deposits; Raisin $396B (with disclosure).
Mean vs median household balance ($62,410 vs $8,000); $330/yr on $8,000 = $1,300 an hour; scales to $800 and $2,000.
Why people do not move: 17 years at one bank, 36% never considered switching, nobody sends the letter.
Curtis's near-loss: promo, tiered and 10%-on-$1,000 traps.
Apps are not banks: Synapse collapse, pass-through insurance risk, $45 for 15 bp.
Tax: savings vs Treasury bill, California top bracket 2.2% vs 2.8%; Ohio saver should skip it.
Argue against self: cash is a poor long-term asset; Vanguard 3.9-5.9% forecast; where cash belongs.
Checklist (permanent, whole-balance, chartered, under $250K, tax check) and "say your rate out loud" close.

claim_audit.claim: Run it for a top bracket earner in California. 4.50 in a savings account nets about 2.2% after tax. The same rate from a Treasury bill nets about 2.8 because the state never touches it. That's roughly 27% more after-tax income
claim_audit.stored_text_witness:
Run it for a
top bracket earner in California.
4.50 in a savings account nets about
2.2% after tax. The same rate from a
Treasury bill nets about 2.8 because the
state never touches it. That's roughly
27% more after-tax income
claim_audit.assessment: [INDEPENDENT_CALCULATION_VERIFIED] With 37% federal plus 13.3% California (49.3% combined, assumed), 4.5% nets 2.28% and a 4.5% T-bill nets 2.84%; 2.84/2.28 = 1.25 to 1.27 ("27%", verified within rounding). The comparison actually offered earlier uses 4.15%; FRED DGS1 shows 4.15% on 2026-07-23 and that bill nets 2.61%. The T-bill still wins but by 15% (2.61/2.28), not 27%. T-bill state-tax exemption is recall (federal statute).

topic.analysis: Why savers should move idle cash to high-yield savings or Treasury bills in 2026, how deposit pricing lags rate hikes, and what pitfalls (promo, tiered rates, fintech apps, taxes) to check before moving.
topic.audience_problem: Savers holding cash at big banks earning near zero while inflation runs about 3.5%.
topic.time_sensitivity: High: rates, inflation and Fed path are dated mid-2026; the script says so and gives a checklist.
topic.narrative_angle: The comeback is not rates; it is that you finally looked.
topic.novelty_and_corpus_angle: Test an original savings-gap video that shows the saver's own dollars at three rates, dates every rate to the recording day, and separates rate gap, tax effect and counterparty risk in one table.
topic.competition: Same-channel nearest-age peers in K01; not an independent niche or causal test
